deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Undefined CAM Allocations

In a commercial lease, the Common Area Maintenance (CAM) clause is often the most volatile component of your total occupancy cost. For dental professionals, the primary danger lies in the distinction between routine maintenance and capital improvements. Sophisticated landlords frequently draft CAM provisions that allow them to pass through the costs of structural replacements—such as a new HVAC system, parking lot repaving, or roof replacement—under the guise of routine maintenance. Because dental offices operate on predictable margins with high fixed overhead, an unbudgeted assessment for a building-wide upgrade can instantly jeopardize your practice's solvency.

Furthermore, landlords often include administrative or management fees calculated as a percentage of total operating expenses. Without strict limitations, these fees become a compounding cost that grows alongside your other expenses, effectively creating a hidden tax on your practice. This fee stacking leads to significant budget volatility that is difficult to forecast during your annual financial planning. Another common tactic is the gross-up clause, where landlords adjust expenses to a full-occupancy level, potentially overcharging you for services that are not being utilized at that scale.

Protecting Your Practice's Bottom Line

To mitigate these risks, your lease must contain specific, enforceable protections that separate operational upkeep from long-term asset enhancement. A robust lease should include the following protections:

  • Cumulative annual caps that limit the year-over-year increase of controllable expenses to a fixed percentage.
  • Explicit exclusions for capital expenditures, ensuring that any major replacement is amortized over its useful life with only the annual portion charged to the tenant.
  • Defined limits on management and administrative fees to prevent arbitrary increases or percentage of expense traps.
  • Comprehensive audit rights allowing you to inspect the landlord's books and records to verify the accuracy of annual CAM reconciliations.
  • Clear definitions of controllable versus uncontrollable expenses to prevent utility spikes from being masked as maintenance costs.
